title: Check a water-saving composition in the right order
instructions: Composition practice. The prompt: ‘Write about something you learned at school that you used in another area of your life. Explain what you did and what you learned from the experience.’ Your notes: in mathematics you learned to compare like quantities; at home you recorded how long your showers lasted on five ordinary days, then used a timer on five later days; four of the later showers were shorter; you did not measure the water used or test anyone else. You have eight minutes left to check your composition. You notice that it does not yet explain how the mathematics idea guided your trial, that one sentence describes your bathroom tiles, that the result comes before the method, and that you wrote ‘five later day’. Check by task, order, content, then sentences.

parts.prompt: Which problem should you fix first?

options.text: Your composition never explains how the mathematics idea guided your home trial.
One comma is missing from the second sentence of the second paragraph of your composition.
The word ‘duration’ appears in two neighbouring sentences.
One sentence could be a little shorter.

choice_rationales.A: The prompt asks how the school learning was used, so this part of the task is missing.
choice_rationales.B: A missing comma is a final-pass correction.
choice_rationales.C: Repeating a word is a small style point.
choice_rationales.D: Sentence length is polish, not a missing part of the task.

parts.hint: Start with whether your composition answers the prompt.
parts.correct_explanation: Completing the task comes before any polishing.

parts.prompt: Which focus sentence best centres your composition?

options.text: Water matters to everyone, so every family in every town should save as much water as possible.
Mathematics has many different topics.
Learning to compare like quantities helped me design a small, fair test of my shower routine.
Timers are the greatest invention.

choice_rationales.A: It is a general opinion and does not mention the school skill.
choice_rationales.B: It names the subject but not the skill or how you used it.
choice_rationales.C: It links the school skill to its use at home and hints at the trial's small size.
choice_rationales.D: It is an unsupported opinion unrelated to the prompt.

parts.hint: State the school skill and where you used it.
parts.correct_explanation: The focus sentence should connect the school learning to the home trial.

options.text: Result → classroom lesson → method → what I learned → a new, unrelated story about my cousin
Classroom idea → ordinary-day record → timer trial → result and its limit → what I learned
Limit → unrelated story → result
What I learned → result → new claim

choice_rationales.A: The result comes before the method, and the ending wanders off.
choice_rationales.B: Each stage prepares the reader for the next.
choice_rationales.C: Key stages are missing, and the order is confusing.
choice_rationales.D: The method is missing, so the reader cannot judge the result.

parts.hint: Give the reader the method before the evidence it produced.
parts.correct_explanation: Putting the method before the result helps the reader understand the evidence.

options.text: I recorded how long my showers lasted on five ordinary days.
I then used a timer on five later days.
Four of the later showers were shorter than my ordinary-day records.
Our bathroom tiles have a blue wave pattern.

choice_rationales.A: This is part of the method.
choice_rationales.B: This is part of the method.
choice_rationales.D: The tiles do nothing to answer the prompt.

parts.hint: Ask what job each detail does.
parts.correct_explanation: The tile description has no job in this composition.

parts.prompt: Which check belongs in your last pass?

options.text: Check plural endings, such as ‘five later days’.
Add a water-volume figure that you did not measure.
Replace your focus with a new topic.
Move the result before the method.

choice_rationales.A: Plural endings are a sentence-level check for the final pass.
choice_rationales.C: This would undo the task-level work.
choice_rationales.D: This would undo the order you fixed.

parts.hint: Choose a sentence-level check that does not change your ideas.
parts.correct_explanation: Plural endings belong in the final pass.

parts.prompt: Which final version best shows all four checks done?

options.text: Maths is useful. I used a timer. It worked for everyone.

Our blue bathroom is nice, and I have always liked long showers after school. In mathematics I learned many topics, such as fractions and graphs. I bought a timer, and timers save exactly fifty litres of water every day for every family, so everyone in my neighbourhood should use one from now on. Nobody could argue with that.

In mathematics I learned to compare like quantities. I recorded five ordinary shower times, then used a timer on five later days. Four were shorter, which suggested the timer could help my routine, although I had not measured the water used or tested anyone else. The trial taught me to make a small claim from small evidence.
I learned mathematics because showers are important.

choice_rationales.A: It leaves out the method and claims a result for everyone.
choice_rationales.B: It keeps irrelevant details and invents a water figure and a claim about everyone.
choice_rationales.C: It keeps all the notes and their limits, in a clear order.
choice_rationales.D: It confuses the cause and leaves out the trial.

parts.hint: Check the task, the order, the evidence and the sentences.
parts.correct_explanation: The third version keeps every note and its limits.
